title: It's Not That You Disagree — It's That I Think You're Wrong
hook: Polarization research usually assumes we dislike people who believe differently. Four studies suggest the sting comes from something narrower: believing the other person is factually mistaken.
key_points: Across four studies with more than 2,000 U.S. adults, what predicted distress was not belief difference but perceived incorrectness.
Participants who saw another's belief as incorrect reported feeling more disturbed, frustrated and upset than those who saw it as merely different.
The more confident participants were that a view was wrong, the more disturbed they felt — and the more they wanted to avoid the person.
Merely holding a different belief did not predict avoidance in less intimate relationships; perceived error did.
In one study the same information was reframed as a neighbor's 'different' versus 'incorrect' belief — the framing alone moved reactions.
The authors' warning: arguing from facts can convert a dispute over priorities into a dispute over who is right.
content_html: Most accounts of political polarization start from a simple premise: we're drawn to people who share our beliefs and repelled by people who don't. Psychologist Andras Molnar and economist George Loewenstein, writing in The Conversation, report evidence that this premise is slightly off — and that the correction matters.
extra_html: Across four studies with more than 2,000 U.S. adults, they found that what made disagreement painful was not difference but perceived error. Participants recalled real disagreements, rated hypothetical social-media posts opposing their views on topics like climate change, capital punishment and policing, and read a fictional narrative in which a neighbor's belief was framed either as "different" or as "incorrect." The pattern held across all three designs: people who regarded another's belief as incorrect reported feeling more disturbed, frustrated and upset, and the more confident they were that the belief was wrong, the worse they felt. Perceived error also predicted wanting to avoid the person — while merely holding a different belief did not, at least in less intimate relationships. The authors draw an uncomfortable practical implication: when people marshal facts to defend preferences, tastes or values, they may convert a disagreement over priorities into a dispute over who is right and who is wrong, which is much harder to live with than a difference of opinion. (U.S. samples; the studies measure reported reactions, not real-world behavior.)

source.name: The Conversation
authors: Andras Molnar, Assistant Professor of Psychology, University of Michigan
George Loewenstein, Professor of Economics and Psychology, Carnegie Mellon University

related.title: Voting Against, Not For
related.hook: Many voters no longer back a candidate they admire — they vote to keep the other party out. That 'negative partisanship' can make even scandal forgivable.

related.hook: Red places get redder and blue places get bluer. Is it because people move to match their politics — or is politics just one reason among many?

related.title: The Poll Behind the Headlines: More Agreement Than It Looks
related.hook: Ask Americans about the country's 250th anniversary and you get a partisan split. Ask about the country's founding ideals and something odd happens: the numbers converge.

related.title: Public Opinion & Polling
related.hook: What 'the people' think shapes what governments do — but measuring it is trickier than it looks, and a bad poll can mislead as easily as a good one informs.

flashcards.prompt: In these four studies, what best predicted how disturbed people felt about someone else's political view?

choices.text: Believing the view was factually incorrect
Simply holding a different view from their own
How strongly they identified with a political party

flashcards.explanation_html: Perceived incorrectness — not mere difference — drove reports of feeling disturbed, frustrated and upset, and predicted wanting to avoid the person.

flashcards.prompt: How did the researchers show that framing alone changes reactions to a disagreement?
flashcards.back_html: Participants read identical information about a neighbor's belief, framed either as different or as incorrect — and reacted worse to the "incorrect" framing.

flashcards.prompt: Why do the authors think arguing from facts can backfire in political disagreement?

choices.text: It can turn a dispute over priorities and values into a dispute over who is right and who is wrong
Because facts are irrelevant to political questions
Because people cannot tell the difference between facts and opinions

flashcards.explanation_html: Once a disagreement is reframed as one side being factually mistaken, it stops being negotiable — which is what makes it emotionally intolerable.
